analysis.one_liner: Tightens SEC oversight of credit rating agencies and lets investors sue over sloppy or conflicted ratings.
analysis.headline: The credit rating reform bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Securities and Exchange Commission to review how credit rating agencies decide their ratings, forced the agencies to set up conflict-of-interest rules and compliance officers, and made them publish how accurate their ratings actually turn out to be. It would also have made it easier for investors to sue an agency that knowingly or recklessly failed to check the facts behind a rating. The bill was filed in July 2009, after the financial crisis showed that agencies had stamped top ratings on risky mortgage investments, and it never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors whose savings, pensions, and 401(k)s ride on credit ratings. When agencies rate bonds and mortgage securities accurately and can be sued for failing to check the facts, investors get a truer picture of risk. Anyone who buys a home or borrows also benefits indirectly, because accurate ratings keep credit markets from mispricing risk the way they did before the 2008 crisis.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, pension savers, and ordinary borrowers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the SEC to review each rating agency's internal controls, ratings, and methods to confirm the agency follows its own rules and that its public disclosures match its actual practices.

Directs the SEC to write rules prohibiting or requiring disclosure of conflicts of interest, including rules barring an agency from rating a structured product that it had previously advised the issuer on how to structure.
Requires each agency to designate a compliance officer who reports on conflicts and internal controls, and to publicly disclose ratings performance so investors can compare accuracy across agencies.

Makes it easier to sue a rating agency for damages by allowing a case to proceed when it shows the agency knowingly or recklessly failed to reasonably investigate or verify the facts its own methodology relied on.

analysis.who_pays: The major credit rating agencies, which would bear the cost of new SEC reviews, compliance staff, public performance disclosures, and a heightened risk of lawsuits from investors. The bill assumes some of these costs would be reflected in the fees agencies charge bond issuers, which could marginally raise borrowing costs for issuers and flow through to investors.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the basic 'issuer pays' business model intact: the company being rated pays the agency for the rating, which is the root conflict of interest the financial crisis exposed. The bill only directs the SEC to write conflict rules and orders a study of alternative ways of paying agencies, rather than changing the structure itself.

Easier lawsuits against rating agencies could push agencies toward overly cautious or defensive ratings practices, and could raise the cost of rating services, costs that may be passed through to bond issuers.

The bill keeps regulators from approving rating methodologies, a deliberate choice to keep agencies accountable for their own models, but that means the SEC reviews processes and disclosures rather than judging whether the models themselves are sound.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, concrete protections: required conflict-of-interest management, a ban on rating products the agency helped structure, public accuracy scorecards, and a workable legal standard for lawsuits. Its main weakness is that it stops short of fixing the underlying payment structure, relying on SEC rules and a future study instead. On balance it was a credible reform whose costs fall mainly on the agencies that had just failed the public, not on ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Rooney introduced the Rating Accountability and Transparency Enhancement Act on July 14, 2009, aiming it at the credit rating agencies whose inflated ratings of mortgage securities had helped trigger the financial crisis.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which was the only action ever taken on it.
No member joined as a cosponsor, the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill was never brought to the House floor before the Congress expired in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major credit rating agencies, which avoided the SEC reviews, conflict-of-interest rules, public accuracy disclosures, and investor lawsuits the bill would have imposed on them.

for.name: Rep. Thomas J. Rooney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the RATE Act on July 14, 2009 and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, and its sole sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern on the merits can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Credit rating agencies (the nationally recognized statistical rating organizations, e.g. Moody's, S&P, Fitch)
industries.note: The bill would have subjected these agencies to mandatory SEC reviews of their ratings and controls, required conflict-of-interest rules including a ban on rating products they had advised on, forced public disclosure of ratings accuracy and client fees, and lowered the legal bar for investors to sue them for damages. The agencies' business model depends on ratings paid for by the issuers they rate, which runs against the public's interest in accurate, independent ratings.
